description: Develop game design skills for students in school to learn space
summary:
I developed Orbital Architect: NASA Mission Design Lab, an interactive space mission design and simulation game modeled on NASA’s Mission Design Lab and Concept Maturity Level (CML) frameworks. Players architect complete missions across five scenarios—from Earth climate monitoring and lunar ice prospecting to Europa exploration and an open sandbox—complete with live CAD spacecraft visualizations, animated orbital telemetry, and post-mission engineering reports.

The game addresses the challenge by dynamically coupling five competing engineering budgets: mass, power and eclipse survival, cost, data downlink, and reliability. Upgrading scientific instruments immediately stresses launch capacity, power margins, and communications, forcing realistic trade-offs. In 2–4 player Team Mode, participants assume specialized roles (Principal Investigator, Systems Engineer, Flight Dynamics Lead, and Mission Ops Lead) to resolve resource conflicts and navigate mid-mission anomalies.

This project is important because aerospace concepts are typically taught in isolation. By turning multidisciplinary systems engineering into an intuitive, collaborative simulation linked to real NASA heritage missions, Orbital Architect bridges textbook theory and practical mission formulation for aspiring engineers.
details:
How It Works

Orbital Architect: NASA Mission Design Lab (v4.2) is a browser-based strategy game that puts players in charge of designing, launching, and operating a real space mission. Players can play solo or team up with 2–4 friends across five difficulty levels—from a beginner Earth-climate satellite to a deep-space mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa, plus a free-play Sandbox mode.

  • Balancing Five Real Engineering Limits: Just like real aerospace engineers, players must keep five competing budgets in balance:
    • Mass: Making sure the spacecraft isn't too heavy for the chosen rocket.
    • Power & Eclipse Survival: Generating enough solar or nuclear power—and packing enough batteries—to survive when the spacecraft passes into a planet's shadow.
    • Budget: Keeping parts, testing, and launch costs under the mission's funding cap.
    • Data Downlink: Making sure the radio antenna is strong enough to send all collected science data back to Earth.
    • Reliability: Protecting the spacecraft against deep-space radiation and hardware failures using backup systems and shielding.
  • Team Negotiation (2–4 Players): In multiplayer mode, each player takes on a real NASA role—Principal Investigator, Spacecraft Systems Engineer, Flight Dynamics Lead, or Mission Ops & Comms Lead. Everyone must approve the design, and when the team runs out of mass, power, or money, a built-in negotiation tool helps players agree on quick compromises.
  • Live Launch & Mission Debrief: Once the design is locked in, players watch an animated rocket launch and live orbital flight. Mid-mission, an unexpected emergency forces players to make a quick engineering decision. Afterward, a NASA-style report grades the mission, explains what went right or wrong, and matches the player's spacecraft to real NASA missions (such as PACE, LRO, JWST, or Europa Clipper).

Benefits & Intended Impact

In school, aerospace engineering is usually taught one formula at a time—students rarely get to see how changing one part affects the rest of the spacecraft.

  • See the Domino Effect: Players immediately experience how adding a powerful camera increases science rewards, while simultaneously making the spacecraft heavier, draining the battery, and overloading the radio antenna.
  • Easy to Start, Deep to Master: Beginners can start with guided Earth-orbit missions using plain-language tips, while advanced students can tackle deep-space radiation, extreme cold, and complex multi-instrument flagships.
  • Teamwork & Real-World Compromise: Multiplayer mode turns engineering into a team negotiation, teaching students that great missions come from smart compromises rather than unlimited budgets.
  • Built for Any Classroom: By running inside any standard web browser, Orbital Architect brings hands-on NASA mission design to classrooms, STEM clubs, and aspiring engineers anywhere in the world.

Tools, Languages & NASA Resources Used

  • Web Standards: Built cleanly using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript for a responsive mission-control interface.
  • Live Spacecraft & Flight Graphics: Uses dynamic SVG graphics to draw and update the spacecraft blueprint in real time, paired with HTML5 Canvas to animate rocket launches, orbits, and live telemetry charts.
  • Zero-Setup Architecture: Built as a lightweight, self-contained web app that runs instantly on school Chromebooks, laptops, and tablets—no downloads, accounts, or servers needed.
  • Real NASA Methodologies & Data: Grounded in NASA’s Systems Engineering Four-Segment Model, JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–4), NASA Mission Design Lab practices, GMAT trajectory concepts, CubeSat 101, and real technical specs from Europa Clipper, James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), and PACE.
  • AI Development & Documentation Support (Google Gemini): Used Google Gemini as an engineering and documentation assistant during the hackathon to help debug HTML5 Canvas and SVG rendering code, verify JavaScript subsystem trade-off calculations, and refine clear, accessible explanations for our project documentation. All core game architecture, NASA mission scenarios, physics rules, and final code testing were designed and validated by our team.

Creativity & Key Design Considerations

  • Visual Engineering Instead of Spreadsheets: Instead of staring at rows of numbers, players watch their spacecraft transform on screen—solar wings stretch wider, nuclear power fins attach, and satellite dishes grow as they adjust parts.
  • Real Space Physics: The simulation uses actual space physics, such as sunlight dropping to just 3.7% strength at Jupiter (forcing players to weigh huge solar arrays against nuclear power), battery drain during orbital night, and radiation damage.
  • More Than One Way to Win: There is no single "correct" build. Players can succeed with a small, low-cost satellite or a massive deep-space observatory, as long as every engineering margin stays safe.
  • Helpful Diagnostics Over Simple "Pass/Fail": When a mission fails, the report explains the exact root cause (such as running out of battery in the Moon's shadow) and shows how a real NASA mission solved that exact challenge.
